title: Analytic Hardy Spaces and Canonical Factorisation

items.title: Analytic Hardy spaces on the unit disc
items.statement: Assume [[def-countable-choice|countable choice]]. Identify the torus $\mathbb T=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with the Euclidean unit circle through $\varphi([t])=e^{2\pi it}$ and let $m$ be its normalized Haar measure ([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]]). For a function $f:\mathbb D\to\mathbb C$ and $0\le r<1$ write $f_r:\mathbb T\to\mathbb C$, $f_r(\zeta):=f(r\zeta)$. For $0<p<\infty$ define $$H^p(\mathbb D):=\Bigl\{\,f\ \text{holomorphic on}\ \mathbb D:\ \|f\|_{H^p}:=\sup_{0\le r<1}\Bigl(\int_{\mathbb T}|f(r\zeta)|^p\,dm(\zeta)\Bigr)^{1/p}<+\infty\,\Bigr\},$$ and for $p=\infty$ define $H^\infty(\mathbb D):=\{f\ \text{holomorphic on}\ \mathbb D:\ \|f\|_\infty:=\sup_{z\in\mathbb D}|f(z)|<+\infty\}$. For $1\le p\le\infty$, $\|\cdot\|_{H^p}$ is a norm on the complex vector space $H^p(\mathbb D)$; for $0<p<1$ it is a quasi-norm with $\|f+g\|_{H^p}\le 2^{1/p-1}(\|f\|_{H^p}+\|g\|_{H^p})$ and $\|\lambda f\|_{H^p}=|\lambda|\,\|f\|_{H^p}$, and $\|f\|_{H^p}=0$ implies $f=0$ because $|f|$ is continuous. This item defines the classes and their (quasi-)norms only; the monotonicity of the radial means and the containments $H^q(\mathbb D)\subseteq H^p(\mathbb D)$ for $q>p$ are proved in [[lem-hardy-radial-means-are-monotone]]. No choice principle beyond countable choice is used.
items.strategy: Assemble the published complex $L^p$ conventions on the probability space $(\mathbb T,m)$; the suprema are finite or $+\infty$ and the vector-space and (quasi-)norm axioms follow from the published Minkowski and Holder items radius by radius. The separability, completeness and duality of these quasi-Banach spaces are not asserted here and are never used.

references.locator: Properties of H^p spaces, printed pp. 26-28: the radial-mean definition of H^p(D), the quasi-norm for p<1 and the containment H^q in H^p.

references.title: J. B. Garnett, Bounded Analytic Functions, revised first edition, Chapter II §1

items.title: Radial p-means of a holomorphic function are nondecreasing
items.statement: Let $f:\mathbb D\to\mathbb C$ be holomorphic and let $0<p<\infty$. For all $0<r\le R<1$, $$\int_{\mathbb T}|f(r\zeta)|^p\,dm(\zeta)\le\int_{\mathbb T}|f(R\zeta)|^p\,dm(\zeta).$$ Consequently, for $f\in H^p(\mathbb D)$ the supremum defining $\|f\|_{H^p}$ is the limit of the nondecreasing map $r\mapsto\int_{\mathbb T}|f(r\zeta)|^p\,dm(\zeta)$, so that $\|f\|_{H^p}=\lim_{r\uparrow1}\|f_r\|_{L^p}$. Moreover, for $0<p<q\le\infty$ one has $H^q(\mathbb D)\subseteq H^p(\mathbb D)$ and $\|f\|_{H^p}\le\|f\|_{H^q}$ for every $f\in H^q(\mathbb D)$.
items.strategy: Apply the published Poisson-modification majorization to the subharmonic function $u=|f|^p$ on the disc $D(0,R)$: for $|z|=r\le R$, $u(z)\le\int_{\mathbb T}P((r/R)\zeta,\eta)u(R\eta)\,dm(\eta)$; integrate in $\zeta$ and use the unit mass of the kernel and Fubini. The containment is Holder with respect to the probability measure $m$.

references.locator: Properties of H^p spaces, printed pp. 26-28 and Jensen section, printed pp. 32-34: monotone radial means and the containment H^q(D) in H^p(D).

items.title: The zero set of a Hardy function satisfies the Blaschke condition
items.statement: Let $f$ be holomorphic on $\mathbb D$ with $f\not\equiv0$, and suppose that $\liminf_{r\uparrow1}\int_{\mathbb T}\log|f(r\zeta)|\,dm(\zeta)<+\infty$. This hypothesis holds in particular for every $f\in H^p(\mathbb D)$, $0<p\le\infty$: Jensen's inequality and [[lem-hardy-radial-means-are-monotone]] give $\int_{\mathbb T}\log|f_r|\,dm\le\log\|f\|_{H^p}$ for $0<p<\infty$ and $\int_{\mathbb T}\log|f_r|\,dm\le\log\|f\|_\infty$ for $p=\infty$. Let $(a_n)_{n\ge1}$ be the zeros of $f$ in $\mathbb D$ repeated according to multiplicity. Then $f$ has only finitely many zeros at the origin, and the nonzero zeros satisfy $$\sum_{n:\,a_n\ne0}\log\frac1{|a_n|}<+\infty,\qquad\text{hence}\qquad \sum_{n\ge1}(1-|a_n|)<+\infty.$$ (The second inequality uses $\log(1/x)\ge1-x$ for $0<x\le1$. The sum may contain the finitely many terms with $a_n=0$, which contribute $1$ each and do not affect convergence of the nonzero part.)
items.strategy: Divide by the power of $z$ at the origin to reduce to $f(0)\ne0$. For each $r<1$ apply the published Jensen formula to $z\mapsto f(rz)$ on the unit disc: $\log|f(0)|=\int_{\mathbb T}\log|f_r|\,dm-\sum_{|a_n|<r}\log(r/|a_n|)$, so the zero sum equals $\int_{\mathbb T}\log|f_r|\,dm-\log|f(0)|\le\log\|f\|_{H^p}-\log|f(0)|$; let $r\uparrow1$ and use monotone convergence (the sums increase) to conclude. Jensen's inequality for the concave logarithm (from the published convex Jensen inequality applied to $-\log$) bounds the mean of $\log|f_r|$ by $\log\|f_r\|_p$. No zeros are lost: a nonzero holomorphic function has isolated zeros, so each disc $|z|<r$ contains finitely many.

references.title: R. K. Srivastava, Lecture Notes on Hardy Spaces (MA650, IIT Guwahati), §5.6, §5.8
references.locator: Jensen's inequality and Jensen's formula, printed pp. 32-34, and Lemma 5.17 (Blaschke condition), printed p. 35: the zero sum bound and $\log(1/|a_n|)\sim(1-|a_n|)$.

references.title: J. B. Garnett, Bounded Analytic Functions, revised first edition, Chapter II §2
references.locator: Blaschke products, printed pp. 51-52: the disc Jensen formula and the Blaschke condition for the zeros of a nonzero H^p function.

items.title: Blaschke factors and Blaschke products
items.statement: For $a\in\mathbb D$ let $\varphi_a(z)=\frac{a-z}{1-\overline a z}$ be the published Blaschke factor ([[def-unit-disc-upper-half-plane-and-blaschke-factor]]), a biholomorphic self-map of $\mathbb D$. Define the normalized Blaschke factor $$b_a(z):=\frac{\overline a}{|a|}\,\varphi_a(z)\ \ (a\ne0),\qquad b_0(z):=z.$$ Then $b_a$ is holomorphic on an open neighbourhood of the closed disc $\overline{\mathbb D}$, has the unique zero $a$ in $\mathbb D$, satisfies $b_a(0)=|a|\ge0$, and $|b_a(\zeta)|=1$ for every $\zeta\in\mathbb T$: for $|\zeta|=1$, $|a-\zeta|=|\overline\zeta-\overline a|=|1-\overline a\zeta|$. A sequence $(a_n)_{n\ge1}$ in $\mathbb D$ is a Blaschke sequence if $\sum_n(1-|a_n|)<+\infty$; its Blaschke product is the holomorphic product $$B(z):=\prod_{n\ge1}b_{a_n}(z)$$ defined as the locally uniform limit of the partial products $B_N:=\prod_{n\le N}b_{a_n}$; for the empty sequence set $B:=1$. This definition is meaningful because the product converges normally on $\mathbb D$: for every $a\in\mathbb D$ and $|z|\le r<1$ one has $$|1-b_a(z)|=\frac{(1-|a|)\,|1+\frac{\overline a}{|a|}z|}{|1-\overline a z|}\le(1-|a|)\frac{1+r}{1-r},$$ so $\sum_n\sup_{|z|\le r}|1-b_{a_n}(z)|\le\frac{1+r}{1-r}\sum_n(1-|a_n|)<+\infty$ and the published normal-convergence theorem applies; the limit $B$ is holomorphic, has exactly the zeros $a_n$ with the multiplicity with which they occur, and satisfies $|B(z)|\le1$. The product does not depend on the enumeration. The boundary-modulus property $|B^*|=1$ a.e. is not part of the definition; it is proved in [[thm-blaschke-product-boundary-values-and-zeros]].
items.strategy: Record the elementary modulus identity and the factor estimate as part of the definition, then invoke the published criterion for normal convergence of holomorphic products; the zero and boundedness clauses are clauses of the cited convergence theorem. Justify the well-definedness (normal convergence, zeros, bound) by the cited boundary-values theorem where referenced.

references.title: J. B. Garnett, Bounded Analytic Functions, revised first edition, Chapter II §2
references.locator: Blaschke products, printed pp. 51-53: the estimate $|1-b_n(z)|\le(1-|z_n|)(1+|z|)/(1-|z|)$, normal convergence, $|B|\le1$ and the zeros of B.

references.title: R. K. Srivastava, Lecture Notes on Hardy Spaces (MA650, IIT Guwahati), §5.8
references.locator: Blaschke Product, printed pp. 35-37: the normalized factor $b_\lambda$, the convergence of the product and the zero set.

items.title: Boundary values and zeros of a Blaschke product
items.statement: Let $(a_n)_{n\ge1}$ be a Blaschke sequence with Blaschke product $B=\prod_n b_{a_n}$ and partial products $B_N$, and let $(a_n)_{n>N}$ be the tail. Then: (i) $|B(z)|\le1$ for every $z\in\mathbb D$, and the zeros of $B$ are exactly the points $a_n$, with multiplicity; (ii) $B/B_N$ is the Blaschke product of the tail, is holomorphic and zero-free on $\mathbb D$, satisfies $|(B/B_N)(z)|\le1$, and $(B/B_N)(0)=\prod_{n>N}|a_n|>0$, which tends to $1$ as $N\to\infty$; (iii) $B$ has finite nontangential limits $B^*(\zeta)$ for $m$-almost every $\zeta\in\mathbb T$, and $|B^*(\zeta)|=1$ for $m$-almost every $\zeta$. In particular $B\not\equiv0$.
items.strategy: (i) and (ii) are clauses of the definition and of the published normal-convergence theorem. For (iii): $B$ is bounded and holomorphic, so its real and imaginary parts are bounded harmonic and the published bounded-harmonic Fatou theorem gives nontangential limits a.e., with $|B^*|\le1$. For the reverse inequality fix $N$ and put $h:=B/B_N$; then $|h(0)|=\prod_{n>N}|a_n|$ and, since $|h|$ is subharmonic, the Poisson-modification majorization gives $|h(0)|\le\int_{\mathbb T}|h(r\zeta)|\,dm(\zeta)$ for every $0<r<1$; let $r\uparrow1$ and use dominated convergence (with $|h|\le1$ and $h_r\to h^*$ a.e., $|B_N|=1$ on $\mathbb T$ so $|h^*|=|B^*|$) to get $\prod_{n>N}|a_n|\le\int_{\mathbb T}|B^*|\,dm\le1$. Letting $N\to\infty$ gives $\int_{\mathbb T}|B^*|\,dm=1$, and since $|B^*|\le1$ a.e. this forces $|B^*|=1$ a.e.

references.locator: Blaschke products, printed pp. 52-53: the argument $|B/B_n(0)|\le\int|B(e^{i\theta})|\,d\theta/2\pi$ yielding $|B|=1$ a.e.

references.locator: Lemma 5.19 and its proof, printed pp. 36-37: convergence of the product, the zero set, $|B|\le1$ and the a.e. unimodular boundary value.

items.title: F. Riesz factorization of a Hardy-space function
items.statement: Let $0<p<\infty$, let $f\in H^p(\mathbb D)$ with $f\not\equiv0$, let $(a_n)$ be its zero sequence repeated with multiplicity and let $B$ be the associated Blaschke product. Then $g:=f/B$ extends holomorphically to $\mathbb D$ (removable singularities at the $a_n$), $g$ has no zero in $\mathbb D$, $|f(z)|\le|g(z)|$ for every $z\in\mathbb D$, and $$g\in H^p(\mathbb D),\qquad \|g\|_{H^p}=\|f\|_{H^p}.$$
items.strategy: Removability: near $a_n$ the quotient $f/B$ is bounded, because the order of the zero of $f$ at $a_n$ is at least the multiplicity with which $a_n$ occurs in (a) (published removable-singularity characterization). Let $B_N$ be the $N$-th partial product and $g_N:=f/B_N$, holomorphic on $\mathbb D$. For $r<R<1$, monotone radial means give $\int|g_N(r\zeta)|^p dm\le\int|f(R\zeta)|^p|B_N(R\zeta)|^{-p}dm$. Since $B_N$ extends continuously to $\overline{\mathbb D}$ with $|B_N|=1$ on $\mathbb T$, for every $\varepsilon>0$ and all $R$ close enough to $1$ one has $|B_N(R\zeta)|\ge1-\varepsilon$ on $\mathbb T$; hence $\int|g_N(r\zeta)|^p dm\le(1-\varepsilon)^{-p}\|f\|_{H^p}^p$. Let $N\to\infty$ (monotone convergence, as $|g_N|$ increases to $|g|$), then $r\uparrow1$, then $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, to get $\|g\|_{H^p}\le\|f\|_{H^p}$; the reverse inequality is $|f|\le|g|$, which follows from $|B|\le1$.

references.title: J. B. Garnett, Bounded Analytic Functions, revised first edition, Chapter II §2
references.locator: Blaschke products, printed pp. 53-54: Theorem 2.3, $f=Bg$ with $\|g\|_{H^p}=\|f\|_{H^p}$, via the maximum principle on $|z|=R$.

references.title: R. K. Srivastava, Lecture Notes on Hardy Spaces (MA650, IIT Guwahati), §5.8
references.locator: Corollary 5.20 (F. Riesz), printed p. 37: $f=Bg$ with $g$ zero-free and $\|g\|_p=\|f\|_p$.

items.title: Fatou boundary theorem for analytic Hardy spaces
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $0<p\le\infty$ and $f\in H^p(\mathbb D)$ (the zero function allowed in (a)-(c)). (a) For $m$-almost every $\zeta\in\mathbb T$ the nontangential limit $f^*(\zeta):=\lim_{z\to\zeta,\,z\in\Gamma_A(\zeta)}f(z)$ exists and is finite for every $A>1$, and $f^*\in L^p(\mathbb T,m)$ with $\|f^*\|_p\le\|f\|_{H^p}$. (b) If $p<\infty$ then $\|f_r-f^*\|_p\to0$ as $r\uparrow1$ and $\|f^*\|_p=\|f\|_{H^p}$; for $p=\infty$, $\|f^*\|_\infty=\|f\|_\infty$ and the radial functions converge to $f^*$ weak-star. (c) If $1\le p\le\infty$ then $f=P[f^*]$, the Poisson integral of its boundary function; for $1<p\le\infty$ this is the published representation theorem for harmonic Hardy classes and for $p=1$ it says that the analytic $h^1$ representing measure of $f$ is the absolutely continuous measure $f^*m$ (proved here, without the F. and M. Riesz theorem, from the a.e. limits and the $L^1$ convergence in (b)).
items.strategy:
Case $1<p<\infty$: $f$ is complex harmonic with $f\in h^p$, so the published $h^p$ representation gives a unique $f^*\in L^p$ with $f=P[f^*]$, $\|f\|_{h^p}=\|f^*\|_p$ and $\|f_r-f^*\|_p	o0$; the published Fatou theorem for $L^1$ data gives the nontangential limits. Case $p=\infty$: bounded harmonic real and imaginary parts have the same representation and limits. Case $0<p\le1$: write $f=Bg$ by the Riesz factorization with $g$ zero-free and $\|g\|=\|f\|$; choose an integer $m\ge2$ with $mp>1$ and put $G:=g^{1/m}$ (holomorphic, obtained from a primitive of $g'/g$ on the star-shaped disc, so $G^m=g$). Then $\int|G_r|^{mp}dm=\int|g_r|^pdm\le\|g\|^p_{H^p}$, so $G\in H^{mp}$ with $\|G\|^{mp}_{H^{mp}}=\|g\|^p_{H^p}$, and the case $mp>1$ applies to $G$: nontangential limits $G^*\in L^{mp}$, $\|G_r-G^*\|_{mp}	o0$, $\|G^*\|_{mp}=\|G\|_{H^{mp}}$. Set $f^*:=B^*(G^*)^m$. Then $|f^*|=|G^*|^m\in L^p$, $f_r=B_rG_r^m	o f^*$ a.e. (both factors have a.e. nontangential limits), and the norm identity follows from $\int|f^*|^p=\int|G^*|^{mp}=\|G\|^{mp}_{H^{mp}}=\sup_r\int|G_r|^{mp}=\sup_r\int|g_r|^p=\|g\|^p_{H^p}=\|f\|^p_{H^p}$. items.title: Log-integrability of boundary values (Riesz brothers)
items.statement: Let $0<p\le\infty$ and $f\in H^p(\mathbb D)$ with $f\not\equiv0$, with boundary function $f^*$ as in [[thm-fatou-boundary-theorem-analytic-hardy-spaces]]. Then $\log|f^*|\in L^1(\mathbb T,m)$; equivalently $\int_{\mathbb T}\log|f^*|\,dm>-\infty$. In particular $f^*\ne0$ $m$-almost everywhere, and if $f^*=0$ on a set of positive $m$-measure then $f\equiv0$.
items.strategy: Write $f=Bg$ by the Riesz factorization with $g$ zero-free, choose $m$ with $mp>1$ and $G=g^{1/m}$ as in the Fatou theorem, so $G$ is zero-free and $g=G^m$. Since $\log|G|$ is harmonic, the published mean value property gives $\int\log|G_r|dm=\log|G(0)|$ for every $r$; hence $\int\log|g_r|dm=m\log|G(0)|$ is constant, and $G(0)\ne0$ because $G$ is zero-free. Because $\log|g_r|\to\log|g^*|$ a.e. and $\int\log^+|g_r|dm\le\|g\|_{H^p}^p/p$ is bounded, Fatou's lemma applied to $\log^-|g_r|$ gives $\int\log^-|g^*|dm\le\liminf_r\int\log^-|g_r|dm=\lim_r\bigl(\int\log^+|g_r|dm-m\log|G(0)|\bigr)$, and $\int\log^+|g_r|\to\int\log^+|g^*|$ by uniform integrability (dominated by $|g_r|^p/p$ and the $L^p$ convergence of the Fatou theorem); hence $\int\log|g^*|dm=m\log|G(0)|>-\infty$. Finally $|f^*|=|g^*|$ a.e. because $|B^*|=1$ a.e.

items.title: The Poisson-Jensen inequality for Hardy functions
items.statement: Let $0<p\le\infty$ and $f\in H^p(\mathbb D)$ with $f\not\equiv0$, with boundary function $f^*\in L^p$ as in [[thm-fatou-boundary-theorem-analytic-hardy-spaces]]; by [[lem-hardy-log-integrability-of-boundary-values]] one has $\log|f^*|\in L^1(\mathbb T,m)$. Then for every $z\in\mathbb D$ $$\log|f(z)|\le P[\log|f^*|](z):=\int_{\mathbb T}P(z,\zeta)\,\log|f^*(\zeta)|\,dm(\zeta),$$ with the convention $\log0=-\infty$. In particular $\log|f|$ is majorized on $\mathbb D$ by the harmonic function $P[\log|f^*|]$, and equality holds for every $z$ whenever $f$ is outer in the sense of [[def-inner-singular-inner-and-outer-functions]].
items.strategy: Fix $z\in\mathbb D$ and $0<R<1$ with $|z|<R$, and put $f_R(w):=f(Rw)$; this function is holomorphic on a neighbourhood of the closed unit disc. Apply the published Jensen formula to $f_R\circ\varphi_z$ and then the change of variables $w=\varphi_z(\zeta)$ on $\mathbb T$ (the Blaschke factor is an involution of the circle with $|\varphi_z'(\zeta)|=(1-|z|^2)/|1-\overline z\zeta|^2=P(z,\zeta)$, the published kernel identity) to obtain $\log|f(Rz)|\le\int_{\mathbb T}P(z,\zeta)\log|f(R\zeta)|\,dm(\zeta)$ (the signed zero terms of Jensen are dropped, giving the inequality). Pass to the limit $R\uparrow1$: the left side tends to $\log|f(z)|$; on the right, $\log^+|f(R\zeta)|$ is uniformly integrable (dominated through $|f_R|^p/p$ and the $L^p$ convergence of the Fatou theorem) and Fatou's lemma bounds the $\log^-$ part, while $\log|f^*|\in L^1$ by the cited lemma, so $\limsup_R\int P(z,\zeta)\log|f(R\zeta)|dm\le\int P(z,\zeta)\log|f^*(\zeta)|dm$; the weight $P(z,\cdot)$ is continuous and positive on the compact torus, which is exactly what makes this Fatou step legitimate. The pointwise inequality at $z$ follows. If $f$ is outer, then $\log|f|=P[\log|f^*|]$ holds by the definition of an outer function, which is the equality case.

items.title: Inner, singular inner and outer functions
items.statement: Assume countable choice. For $\zeta\in\mathbb T$ (regarded as a point of the unit circle) and $z\in\mathbb D$ put $$K(z,\zeta):=\frac{\zeta+z}{\zeta-z}.$$ For fixed $z$ the function $\zeta\mapsto K(z,\zeta)$ is bounded and continuous on the compact torus, with $$\operatorname{Re}K(z,\zeta)=\frac{1-|z|^2}{|\zeta-z|^2}=P(z,\zeta)>0,$$ and for fixed $\zeta$ the function $z\mapsto K(z,\zeta)$ is holomorphic on $\mathbb C\setminus\{\zeta\}$. (a) A holomorphic $\theta:\mathbb D\to\mathbb C$ is called an **inner function** if $\theta\in H^\infty(\mathbb D)$ and $|\theta^*(\zeta)|=1$ for $m$-almost every $\zeta\in\mathbb T$, where $\theta^*$ is its boundary function. Every Blaschke product is inner ([[thm-blaschke-product-boundary-values-and-zeros]]), and $|\theta|\le1$ on $\mathbb D$ for every inner $\theta$. (b) For a finite positive Borel measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb T$ define $$S_\mu(z):=\exp\Bigl(-\int_{\mathbb T}K(z,\zeta)\,d\mu(\zeta)\Bigr)\qquad(z\in\mathbb D).$$ If $\mu$ is singular with respect to $m$ ($\mu\perp m$), $S_\mu$ is called a **singular inner function**. The function $S_\mu$ is well defined and holomorphic, has no zeros, satisfies $|S_\mu(z)|=e^{-P[\mu](z)}\le1$ and $S_\mu(0)=e^{-\mu(\mathbb T)}>0$; these and the boundary behaviour are proved in [[thm-singular-inner-function-properties]]. (c) For a nonnegative measurable $h:\mathbb T\to[0,+\infty]$ with $\log h\in L^1(\mathbb T,m)$ define the **outer function** $$[h](z):=\exp\Bigl(\int_{\mathbb T}K(z,\zeta)\,\log h(\zeta)\,dm(\zeta)\Bigr)\qquad(z\in\mathbb D);$$ here $\log h$ is extended by $-\infty$ where $h=0$ and the integral is absolutely convergent because $|K(z,\zeta)|\le\frac{1+|z|}{1-|z|}$ and $|\log h|\in L^1$. The function $[h]$ is holomorphic, has no zeros, satisfies $[h](0)=\exp(\int\log h\,dm)>0$ and depends only on the $m$-class of $h$; if $h\in L^p$ then $[h]\in H^p$ and $|[h]^*|=h$ a.e. ([[lem-outer-function-properties]]). A holomorphic $f$ on $\mathbb D$ is called **outer** if $f=e^{i\gamma}[\,|f^*|\,]$ for some $\gamma\in\mathbb R$; equivalently (cited lemma) if $\log|f^*|\in L^1$ and $\log|f(z)|=P[\log|f^*|](z)$ for every $z\in\mathbb D$. The outer function is determined by $|h|$ up to a unimodular constant and normalized by $[h](0)>0$.
items.strategy: Record the kernel identity from the published Poisson kernel, then define the three classes and cite the two proved items for every asserted property (holomorphy, zero-freeness, bounds, boundary moduli, normalization and uniqueness up to a unimodular constant). No representation theorem for general inner functions is assumed; that is proved later in this pair.

items.title: Properties of the outer function of a boundary modulus
items.statement: Let $0<p\le\infty$, let $h\ge0$ be measurable on $\mathbb T$ with $\log h\in L^1(\mathbb T,m)$ and $h\in L^p(\mathbb T,m)$, and let $[h]$ be the outer function. Then: (i) $[h]$ is holomorphic and zero-free on $\mathbb D$ with $[h](0)=\exp(\int\log h\,dm)>0$, and for $p<\infty$ $$|[h](z)|^p\le P[h^p](z)\quad(z\in\mathbb D);$$ hence $[h]\in H^p(\mathbb D)$ with $\|[h]\|_{H^p}\le\|h\|_p$, while for $p=\infty$ one has $|[h]|\le\|h\|_\infty$ and $[h]\in H^\infty$. (ii) $[h]^*(\zeta)=h(\zeta)$ in modulus: $|[h]^*(\zeta)|=h(\zeta)$ for $m$-a.e. $\zeta$. (iii) If $h_1=h_2$ a.e. then $[h_1]=[h_2]$. (iv) If $g\in H^p$ satisfies $g\not\equiv0$, $|g^*|=h$ a.e. and the outer equality $\log|g(z)|=P[\log h](z)$ for all $z$, then $g=e^{i\gamma}[h]$ for some $\gamma\in\mathbb R$; in particular the outer function with prescribed boundary modulus is determined up to a unimodular constant.
items.strategy: (i) Expand $K(z,\zeta)=1+2\sum_{n\ge1}(z/\zeta)^n$: the exponents' power series has coefficients bounded by $\|\log h\|_1$, so it defines a holomorphic function with $[h](0)=e^{\int\log h}>0$ (published power-series holomorphy), and $[h]=\exp(\text{holomorphic})$ is zero-free. For the pointwise bound apply the published convex Jensen inequality to the probability measure $P(z,\zeta)dm(\zeta)$ and the convex function $e^t$ with $t=p\log h(\zeta)$: $e^{\int P\,p\log h\,dm}\le\int P\,h^p\,dm$; integrating in $\zeta$ on a circle and using Fubini and the unit mass of the kernel gives $\|[h]_r\|_p\le\|h\|_p$. (ii) $\log|[h]|=P[\log h]$ is the Poisson integral of the $L^1$ function $\log h$, so the published Fatou theorem for $L^1$ data gives nontangential limits $\log h$ a.e.; exponentiating gives $|[h]^*|=h$ a.e. (the argument of $[h]$ also converges at the same points by the corresponding limits of the conjugate function, or alternatively apply the Fatou theorem of this pair to $[h]\in H^p$). (iii) is immediate from the definition. (iv) $g/[h]$ is holomorphic and zero-free with modulus identically $1$, hence constant of modulus one by the maximum principle.

items.title: Singular inner functions from finite singular measures
items.statement: Let $\mu$ be a finite positive Borel measure on $\mathbb T$ and let $S_\mu(z)=\exp(-\int_{\mathbb T}K(z,\zeta)d\mu(\zeta))$. Then $S_\mu$ is holomorphic and zero-free on $\mathbb D$, $\log|S_\mu|=-P[\mu]$, $|S_\mu|\le1$, and $S_\mu(0)=e^{-\mu(\mathbb T)}\in(0,1]$. Moreover $S_\mu$ has finite nontangential limits $S_\mu^*(\zeta)$ for $m$-a.e. $\zeta$, with $|S_\mu^*|=e^{-\lim_{r\uparrow1}P[\mu](r\zeta)}$, and the following are equivalent: (i) $\mu\perp m$; (ii) $|S_\mu^*|=1$ a.e.; (iii) $P[\mu](r\zeta)\to0$ for $m$-a.e. $\zeta$. Consequently $S_\mu$ is a singular inner function exactly when $\mu\perp m$.
items.strategy: Holomorphy: differentiate the integral in $z$ (or expand $K$ as a power series with coefficients in $L^1(\mu)$), and $\operatorname{Re}K=P$ gives $\log|S_\mu|=-P[\mu]\le0$. The nontangential limits exist because $S_\mu\in H^\infty$ (published bounded-harmonic Fatou for the real and imaginary parts of the exponent). (i)$\Rightarrow$(iii): $\mu\perp m$ is concentrated on a null set $N$, so for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is an open $U\supseteq N$ with $m(U)<\varepsilon$ and $\mu(\mathbb T\setminus U)=0$; then $P[\mu](z)\le\mu(\mathbb T)\sup_{\zeta\in U}P(z,\zeta)$, and $\sup_{\zeta\in U}P(z,\zeta)\to0$ as $z\to\zeta_0\in\mathbb T\setminus\overline U$ inside any cone, so $P[\mu]\to0$ off $\overline U$; letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ gives (iii). (iii)$\Rightarrow$(ii) is immediate from the displayed limit formula. (ii)$\Rightarrow$(i): decompose $\mu=h\,m+\mu_s$ by the published Lebesgue decomposition and Radon-Nikodym theorem; then $P[h]\le P[\mu]$ and the published Fatou theorem for $L^1$ data gives $P[h](r\zeta)\to h(\zeta)$ a.e.; from $P[\mu]\to0$ a.e. we get $h\le0$ a.e., and $h\ge0$ gives $h=0$ a.e., so $\mu=\mu_s\perp m$.

items.title: Zero-free inner functions are singular inner functions
items.statement: Let $S$ be holomorphic and zero-free on $\mathbb D$ with $|S|\le1$, and suppose that its boundary function satisfies $|S^*|=1$ $m$-a.e. (equivalently, $S$ is an inner function without zeros). Then there are a unique $\lambda\in\mathbb T$ and a unique finite positive measure $\mu\perp m$ with $$S=\lambda\,S_\mu,\qquad S_\mu(z)=\exp\Bigl(-\int_{\mathbb T}K(z,\zeta)d\mu(\zeta)\Bigr).$$ With the normalizations $S_\mu(0)=e^{-\mu(\mathbb T)}>0$ and $\lambda=S(0)/S_\mu(0)$, the pair $(\lambda,\mu)$ is unique. In particular $S_\mu$ is the singular inner function of $\mu$, and every inner function is, up to a unimodular constant, the product of a Blaschke product and a singular inner function.
items.strategy: Since $S$ is zero-free, $u:=-\log|S|$ is a nonnegative harmonic function on $\mathbb D$; by the published Herglotz representation of nonnegative harmonic functions (Harnack convergence theorem) there is a unique finite positive measure $\mu$ with $u=P[\mu]$. The function $H(z):=\int K(z,\zeta)d\mu(\zeta)$ is holomorphic with $\operatorname{Re}H=P[\mu]=u$, so $S e^{H}$ is holomorphic with constant modulus $1$; hence $S e^{H}=\lambda$ for some $\lambda\in\mathbb T$ and $S=\lambda e^{-H}=\lambda S_\mu$. Singularity: $|S^*|=1$ a.e. forces $P[\mu]\to0$ a.e., and the equivalence proved in [[thm-singular-inner-function-properties]] gives $\mu\perp m$. Uniqueness: $\mu$ is determined by $P[\mu]=-\log|S|$ and $\lambda$ by evaluation at $0$.

items.title: Inner-outer factorization in Hardy spaces
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $0<p\le\infty$ and let $f\in H^p(\mathbb D)$ with $f\not\equiv0$, with boundary function $f^*\in L^p$ and $\log|f^*|\in L^1$ (the two preceding items). Then there exist a constant $\lambda\in\mathbb T$, a Blaschke product $B$ (the product of the normalized Blaschke factors of the zeros of $f$), a finite positive measure $\mu\perp m$ with associated singular inner function $S_\mu$, and the outer function $F:=[\,|f^*|\,]$, such that $$f=\lambda\,B\,S_\mu\,F,$$ with $F\in H^p$ and $\|F\|_{H^p}\le\|f\|_{H^p}$, and: $B$ is determined by the zeros of $f$; $F$ is the unique outer function with $F(0)>0$ and $|F^*|=|f^*|$ a.e.; $\mu$ is the unique finite positive singular measure with $S_\mu(0)>0$ and $f/(B S_\mu F)$ constant of modulus $1$; and $\lambda$ is that constant. The factorization is unique in this normalized sense.
items.strategy: Write $f=Bg$ with $g$ zero-free and $\|g\|=\|f\|$ (Riesz factorization) and set $F:=[|f^*|]$ (outer, $\in H^p$ with $|F^*|=|f^*|$ a.e. by the outer-function lemma). Then $S:=g/F$ is holomorphic and zero-free on $\mathbb D$, and the Poisson-Jensen inequality $\log|g|\le P[\log|g^*|]=\log F$ gives $|S|\le1$; moreover $|S^*|=|g^*|/|F^*|=1$ a.e. because $|B^*|=1$ gives $|g^*|=|f^*|$. Hence $S$ is a zero-free inner function, so $S=\lambda'S_\mu$ with $\lambda'\in\mathbb T$ and $\mu\perp m$ unique (zero-free inner theorem); substituting gives $f=\lambda'B S_\mu F$. Uniqueness: the zeros determine $B$; $|F^*|=|f^*|$ together with outer-ness and $F(0)>0$ determines $F$ (outer-function lemma (iv)); then the quotient $f/(B F)$ is a zero-free inner function whose representation $(\lambda,S_\mu)$ is unique. $F\in H^p$ and $\|F\|\le\|f\|$ follow from the pointwise bound $|F|^p\le P[|f^*|^p]$.

items.title: A harmonic majorant of log^+|F| exists exactly when the radial log^+ means are bounded
items.statement: Let $F:\mathbb D\to\mathbb C$ be holomorphic and put $u:=\log^+|F|$. Then $u$ has a harmonic majorant on $\mathbb D$ if and only if $$\sup_{0<r<1}\int_{\mathbb T}\log^+|F(r\zeta)|\,dm(\zeta)<+\infty.$$ The forward implication is immediate from the mean value property of a harmonic majorant; the converse is the Poisson-modification construction below.
items.strategy: ($\Rightarrow$) If $h\ge u$ is harmonic on $\mathbb D$, then $\int_{\mathbb T}\log^+|F(r\zeta)|dm(\zeta)\le\int_{\mathbb T}h(r\zeta)dm(\zeta)=h(0)$ for every $0<r<1$, so the supremum is at most $h(0)<\infty$. ($\Leftarrow$) Suppose $C:=\sup_{0<r<1}\int_{\mathbb T}\log^+|F(r\zeta)|dm(\zeta)<\infty$. First, $u=\max(\log|F|,0)$ is subharmonic: $\log|F|$ is subharmonic and a finite maximum of subharmonic functions is subharmonic, the second function being the subharmonic constant $0$. For $0<r<1$ let $h_r:=P_{D(0,r)}u$ be the Poisson modification of $u$ on the disc $D(0,r)$; by definition $h_r$ is harmonic on $D(0,r)$ and $h_r\ge u$ there. Since $u$ is continuous on every circle, in the boundary-approximation construction of $P_{D(0,r)}u$ one may take $\phi_n:=u|_{|z|=r}+1/n$, so $h_r$ is the ordinary Poisson extension of $u|_{|z|=r}$ to $D(0,r)$, continuous on the closed disc, and $h_r(0)=\int_{\mathbb T}u(r\zeta)dm(\zeta)\le C$. If $0<r<\rho<1$, then $h_\rho\ge u=h_r$ on $\partial D(0,r)$ and both functions are harmonic on $D(0,r)$, so the minimum principle gives $h_\rho\ge h_r$ on $D(0,r)$; hence $r\mapsto h_r(z)$ is increasing on $(|z|,1)$ for every $z\in\mathbb D$. Since $h_r\ge0$, the Harnack inequality on $D(0,r)$ gives $$0\le h_r(z)\le\frac{r+|z|}{r-|z|}\,h_r(0)\le\frac{1+|z|}{1-|z|}\,C\qquad(r>|z|).$$ Fix $R<1$ and $n_0$ with $r_{n_0}:=1-1/n_0>R$. On $D(0,r_{n_0})$ the tail $(h_{r_n})_{n\ge n_0}$ is an increasing sequence of harmonic functions with $h_{r_n}(0)\le C$, so the increasing Harnack convergence principle provides a harmonic limit on $D(0,r_{n_0})$; applying this on each disc $D(0,R)$, $R<1$, and using uniqueness of local limits produces a single harmonic limit $H:=\lim_n h_{r_n}$ on $\mathbb D$. For every $z$ and all $n$ with $r_n>|z|$ one has $h_{r_n}(z)\ge u(z)$, so $H\ge u$. Thus $H$ is a harmonic majorant of $u$.

items.title: The Nevanlinna class on the disc
items.statement: Assume countable choice. A holomorphic function $f:\mathbb D\to\mathbb C$ belongs to the **Nevanlinna class** $N(\mathbb D)$ if the subharmonic function $\log^+|f|$ has a harmonic majorant on $\mathbb D$, that is, if there is a harmonic $h$ on $\mathbb D$ with $$\log^+|f(z)|\le h(z)\qquad(z\in\mathbb D),$$ where $\log^+x=\max\{\log x,0\}$. Since $\log^+|f|\ge0$, any such majorant satisfies $h\ge0$ on $\mathbb D$. Every $H^p(\mathbb D)$, $0<p\le\infty$, is contained in $N(\mathbb D)$: for $0<p<\infty$ one has $\log^+|f|\le|f|^p/p$, so $\log^+|f|$ is bounded, and for $p=\infty$ one has $\log^+|f|\le\log\|f\|_\infty$. (Equivalently, $f\in N(\mathbb D)$ iff $\sup_{0<r<1}\int_{\mathbb T}\log^+|f(r\zeta)|dm(\zeta)<+\infty$; the majorant direction is the mean value property of a harmonic majorant and the converse is [[lem-nevanlinna-sup-mean-criterion]]. Both forms are used in this pair.) This is the disc Nevanlinna class of holomorphic functions. It is unrelated to the Nevanlinna value-distribution theory of meromorphic functions on $\mathbb C$ (counting functions, proximity, characteristic $T(r,f)$, first and second main theorems), which is developed elsewhere in this library; the name is the only overlap, and no result from that theory is used in this pair.
items.strategy: Define the class by the harmonic-majorant condition of the sources; the equivalence with boundedness of the radial $\log^+$ means is proved in [[lem-nevanlinna-sup-mean-criterion]] (majorant $\Rightarrow$ bound by the mean value property; bound $\Rightarrow$ majorant by the Poisson-modification and increasing-Harnack construction). Record the containment $H^p\subseteq N$ as an immediate estimate using the published subharmonicity of $\log|f|$ ([[thm-log-modulus-of-a-holomorphic-function-is-subharmonic]]) and the boundedness of $\log^+|f|$ on $H^p$. Both forms are used by the later items: the majorant form in [[thm-nevanlinna-class-is-bounded-quotient-class]] and [[thm-nevanlinna-boundary-values-and-log-integrability]], the sup-mean form in [[lem-nevanlinna-blaschke-factorization]].

items.title: The Nevanlinna class is a bounded quotient class
items.statement: For a holomorphic $f:\mathbb D\to\mathbb C$ the following are equivalent: (i) $f\in N(\mathbb D)$; (ii) there exist $g,h\in H^\infty(\mathbb D)$ with $h$ zero-free in $\mathbb D$ and $f=g/h$, where in addition $g$ and $h$ may be chosen with $|g|\le1$ and $|h|\le1$. The pair $(g,h)$ is not unique: if $\varphi\in H^\infty$ is zero-free then $(g\varphi,h\varphi)$ is another representation of the same $f$, and no uniqueness is asserted.
items.strategy: For (ii)$\Rightarrow$(i): if $f=g/h$ with $h$ zero-free, normalize $\lambda:=\max\{\|g\|_\infty,\|h\|_\infty,1\}$ and replace $(g,h)$ by $(g/\lambda,h/\lambda)$, which leaves $f$ unchanged and gives $|g|\le1$, $|h|\le1$; then $H:=\log^+\|g\|_\infty+\log^+\|h\|_\infty-\log|h|$ is harmonic on $\mathbb D$ because $h$ is zero-free, satisfies $H\ge0$ because $|h|\le1$ and the two $\log^+$ terms are $\ge0$, and whenever $\log|f|>0$ one has $\log|f|=\log|g|-\log|h|\le\log\|g\|_\infty-\log|h|\le H$; hence $\log^+|f|\le H$ and $H$ is a nonnegative harmonic majorant of $\log^+|f|$. For (i)$\Rightarrow$(ii): let $h_0$ be a harmonic majorant of $\log^+|f|$; then $h_0\ge0$, and by the published Herglotz representation of nonnegative harmonic functions (Harnack convergence theorem, Axiom of Choice) $h_0=P[\sigma]$ for a unique finite positive measure $\sigma$. Let $\widetilde h_0$ be a harmonic conjugate of $h_0$ on the simply connected disc and put $h:=\exp(-h_0-i\widetilde h_0)$; then $h$ is holomorphic, zero-free and $|h|=e^{-h_0}\le1$. For $g:=fh$ one has $|g|=|f|e^{-h_0}\le e^{\log^+|f|}e^{-h_0}\le1$, because $\log|f|\le\log^+|f|\le h_0$; hence $g\in H^\infty$ and $f=g/h$.

items.title: Blaschke factorization of a Nevanlinna-class function
items.statement: Let $f\in N(\mathbb D)$, $f\not\equiv0$, let $(a_n)$ be its zero sequence repeated with multiplicity and let $B$ be the associated Blaschke product. Then $B$ is a Blaschke product in the sense of [[def-blaschke-product]], $g:=f/B$ extends holomorphically to $\mathbb D$ (removable singularities at the $a_n$), $g$ has no zeros in $\mathbb D$, $|f(z)|\le|g(z)|$ on $\mathbb D$, and $g\in N(\mathbb D)$.
items.strategy: Choice of a harmonic majorant $h_0$ of $\log^+|f|$ gives $\int_{\mathbb T}\log|f_r|dm\le\int h_0(r\zeta)dm=h_0(0)<\infty$ by the mean value property, so the zero sequence satisfies the general hypothesis of the Blaschke-condition theorem and $B$ converges normally. The quotient is holomorphic and zero-free as in the Riesz factorization. For $g\in N$: $|g|=|f|/|B|$ with $|B|\le1$, so $\log^+|g|\le\log^+|f|+\log(1/|B|)$ pointwise. For $0<r<1$, $\int_{\mathbb T}\log|B(r\zeta)|dm=\sum_{|a_n|<r}\log r+\sum_{|a_n|\ge r}\log|a_n|$ by the classical factor identity $\int_{\mathbb T}\log|\zeta-c|dm=\log^+|c|$ (a factor with $|a_n|<r$ contributes $\log r$, a factor with $|a_n|\ge r$ contributes $\log|a_n|$, and the boundary case $|a_n|=r$ is the limiting case); hence $\int_{\mathbb T}\log(1/|B(r\zeta)|)dm\le(\log\frac1r)N(r)+\sum_{|a_n|\ge r}(-\log|a_n|)$, where $N(r)=\#\{n:|a_n|<r\}$. For $r\ge1/2$ the right side is at most $2\sum_n(1-|a_n|)+2\sum_n(1-|a_n|)$, using $\log(1/r)\le2(1-r)$ and $N(r)(1-r)\le\sum_n(1-|a_n|)$ for the first term and $\log(1/|a|)\le2(1-|a|)$ for $|a|\ge1/2$ in the tail; this bound $K<\infty$ is uniform for $r\ge1/2$. For $0<r\le1/2$, $g$ is continuous on the compact disc $|z|\le1/2$ after the removable-singularity extension, so $\int_{\mathbb T}\log^+|g(r\zeta)|dm\le\sup_{|z|\le1/2}\log^+|g(z)|<\infty$. Therefore $\sup_{0<r<1}\int_{\mathbb T}\log^+|g(r\zeta)|dm<\infty$, and the sup-mean criterion [[lem-nevanlinna-sup-mean-criterion]] supplies a harmonic majorant of $\log^+|g|$, so $g\in N(\mathbb D)$ by [[def-nevanlinna-class-on-the-disc]].

items.title: Boundary values and log-integrability for the Nevanlinna class
items.statement: Let $f\in N(\mathbb D)$ with $f\not\equiv0$. Then $f$ has finite nontangential limits $f^*(\zeta)$ for $m$-almost every $\zeta\in\mathbb T$, and $\log|f^*|\in L^1(\mathbb T,m)$; in particular $f^*\ne0$ a.e.
items.strategy: Write $f=Bg$ with $g$ zero-free in $N$ (Blaschke factorization lemma). Choose a nonnegative harmonic majorant $h_0$ of $\log^+|g|$ and put $u:=h_0$, $w:=h_0-\log|g|$; both are nonnegative harmonic on $\mathbb D$, because $g$ is zero-free and $\log|g|\le\log^+|g|\le h_0$. By the Herglotz representation $u=P[\sigma]$, $w=P[\tau]$ for finite positive measures, and on the simply connected disc $u,w$ have harmonic conjugates $v,z$, so $g=e^{ic}e^{-(w+iz)}/e^{-(u+iv)}$, a quotient of the two bounded zero-free holomorphic functions $e^{-(w+iz)}$ and $e^{-(u+iv)}$. Each has modulus $\le1$, so the published bounded-harmonic Fatou theorem gives nontangential limits a.e.; the denominator's limit does not vanish a.e. because its modulus is $e^{-u^*}$ and $u^*<\infty$ a.e. (Fatou's lemma: $\int u^*dm\le\liminf_r\int u(r\zeta)dm=u(0)<\infty$). Hence $g$ has nontangential limits a.e., $\log|g^*|=u^*-w^*$, and $\int|\log|g^*||dm\le u(0)+w(0)<\infty$. Multiplying by $B$, whose boundary values are unimodular a.e. (Blaschke theorem), gives the claim for $f$.

items.title: The Smirnov class on the disc
items.statement: Assume countable choice. The **Smirnov class** $N^+(\mathbb D)$ is the set of $f\in N(\mathbb D)$ such that, with $f^*$ the boundary function of [[thm-nevanlinna-boundary-values-and-log-integrability]] (so that $\log|f^*|\in L^1$, extended by $-\infty$ where $f^*=0$), $$\log|f(z)|\le P[\log|f^*|](z)\qquad\text{for every }z\in\mathbb D.$$ The zero function is included (for it $\log|f|=-\infty$). By the Poisson-Jensen inequality every $f\in H^p(\mathbb D)$, $0<p\le\infty$, lies in $N^+(\mathbb D)$ with equality in the displayed inequality, so $H^p(\mathbb D)\subseteq N^+(\mathbb D)\subseteq N(\mathbb D)$. Equivalently, $N^+(\mathbb D)$ is the class of quotients $g/h$ with $g,h\in H^\infty(\mathbb D)$ and $h$ outer (and then $h$ may be normalized by $h(0)>0$); this equivalence is proved in [[lem-smirnov-class-quotient-characterisation]].
items.strategy: Use the inequality characterization (c) of the source's Theorem 5.4 as the definition; the containment $H^p\subseteq N^+$ is exactly the Poisson-Jensen inequality of this pair, and $N^+\subseteq N$ is the definition. The quotient characterization is proved in the cited lemma.

items.title: The Smirnov class as a class of quotients with outer denominator
items.statement: Let $f$ be holomorphic on $\mathbb D$ with $f\not\equiv0$. Then $f\in N^+(\mathbb D)$ if and only if there are $g,h\in H^\infty(\mathbb D)$ with $h$ outer (equivalently $\log|h^*|\in L^1$ and $\log|h(z)|=P[\log|h^*|](z)$ for all $z$) such that $f=g/h$. Moreover $h$ may be chosen with $h(0)>0$ and $|h|\le1$, and the representation is not unique: $(g,h)$ may be replaced by $(g\varphi,h\varphi)$ for any zero-free $\varphi\in H^\infty$.
items.strategy: ($\Leftarrow$) If $f=g/h$ with $g,h\in H^\infty$ and $h$ outer, then the Poisson-Jensen inequality gives $\log|g|\le P[\log|g^*|]$ and outer-ness gives $\log|h|=P[\log|h^*|]$; subtracting gives $\log|f|\le P[\log|f^*|]$, so $f\in N^+$ (and $f\in N$ by the quotient theorem). ($\Rightarrow$) Let $f\in N^+$, so $\log|f^*|\in L^1$; put $\varphi:=\log^+|f^*|+1\in L^1$, $\varphi\ge0$, and $h:=[e^{-\varphi}]$, an outer function with $0<h(0)=e^{-\int\varphi}\le1$ and $|h|=e^{-P[\varphi]}\le1$, hence $h\in H^\infty$ outer. Then $g:=fh$ satisfies $\log|g|=\log|f|-P[\varphi]\le P[\log|f^*|-\varphi]=P[-\log^-|f^*|-1]\le-1$, so $|g|\le e^{-1}$ and $g\in H^\infty$; then $f=g/h$ with $h$ outer, $h(0)>0$, $|h|\le1$. Non-uniqueness is multiplication of numerator and denominator by a common zero-free bounded factor.

items.title: The Smirnov maximum principle: N+ intersected with Lp is Hp
items.statement: Let $0<p\le\infty$ and let $f\in N^+(\mathbb D)$ with boundary function $f^*$. If $f^*\in L^p(\mathbb T,m)$ then $f\in H^p(\mathbb D)$ and $$\|f\|_{H^p}=\|f^*\|_p\quad(0<p<\infty),\qquad \|f\|_\infty=\|f^*\|_\infty.$$ Consequently a function of $N^+(\mathbb D)$ lies in $H^p(\mathbb D)$ exactly when its boundary function lies in $L^p$, with equality of norms; this is written $N^+\cap L^p=H^p$. (The statement is false with $N$ in place of $N^+$: the reciprocal $1/S_\mu$ of a nonconstant singular inner function lies in $N$ with unimodular boundary values, but is not bounded on $\mathbb D$ and hence not in $H^\infty$.)
items.strategy: For $p<\infty$ the defining inequality of $N^+$ together with the published convex Jensen inequality applied to the probability measure $P(z,\zeta)dm(\zeta)$ and the convex function $t\mapsto e^{pt}$ gives $|f(z)|^p\le\int P(z,\zeta)|f^*(\zeta)|^pdm(\zeta)=P[|f^*|^p](z)$ for every $z$; integrating over a circle and using the unit mass of the kernel (Fubini/Tonelli) gives $\int|f(r\zeta)|^pdm\le\int|f^*|^pdm$ for all $r$, so $f\in H^p$ with $\|f\|_{H^p}\le\|f^*\|_p$. Fatou's lemma gives the reverse inequality $\|f^*\|_p\le\liminf_r\|f_r\|_p\le\|f\|_{H^p}$ because $f_r\to f^*$ a.e.; hence equality, and the boundary function supplied by the Fatou theorem of this pair equals $f^*$ a.e. by uniqueness of a.e. limits. For $p=\infty$ the same estimates give $|f|\le\|f^*\|_\infty$ and $\|f^*\|_\infty\le\|f\|_\infty$.

items.title: Analytic Poisson integrals are exactly the measures with vanishing negative coefficients
items.statement: Let $\mu$ be a finite complex Borel measure on $\mathbb T$ and let $\widehat\mu(n):=\int_{\mathbb T}\zeta^{-n}\,d\mu(\zeta)$, $n\in\mathbb Z$. The following are equivalent: (i) $P[\mu]$ is holomorphic on $\mathbb D$; (ii) $P[\mu](z)=\sum_{n\ge0}\widehat\mu(n)z^n$ for $|z|<1$, the power series obtained from the Poisson kernel expansion, with no negative powers of $z$; (iii) $\widehat\mu(n)=0$ for every $n<0$. When these hold, $P[\mu]\in H^1(\mathbb D)$ with $\|P[\mu]\|_{H^1}\le|\mu|(\mathbb T)$, and its Taylor coefficients are the $\widehat\mu(n)$, $n\ge0$.
items.strategy: The Poisson kernel has the locally uniformly convergent expansion $P(z,\zeta)=\sum_{n\ge0}z^n\zeta^{-n}+\sum_{n<0}\overline z^{\,-n}\zeta^{-n}$ for $|z|<1$, $|\zeta|=1$; integrating termwise against $\mu$ (dominated convergence for the counting measure, with $|\widehat\mu(n)|\le|\mu|(\mathbb T)$) gives $P[\mu](z)=\sum_{n\ge0}\widehat\mu(n)z^n+\sum_{n<0}\widehat\mu(n)\overline z^{\,-n}$, so (iii) is equivalent to (ii), and (ii) implies (i) by the published holomorphy of power series. Conversely, if $P[\mu]$ is holomorphic with Taylor coefficients $a_k$, then for $0<r<1$ and $n<0$ the Fourier coefficient identity $r^{|n|}\widehat\mu(n)=\int_{\mathbb T}P[\mu](r\zeta)\zeta^{-n}dm(\zeta)$, read off from the same expansion, combines with $\int_{\mathbb T}P[\mu](r\zeta)\zeta^{-n}dm(\zeta)=0$ (the integrand is $\sum_{k\ge0}a_kr^k\zeta^{k-n}$ and $k-n>0$ for every $k\ge0$) to give $\widehat\mu(n)=0$; hence (i) implies (iii). The $H^1$ bound follows from $|P[\mu](z)|\le\int P(z,\zeta)\,d|\mu|(\zeta)$, the unit mass of the kernel on each circle and Fubini.

items.title: The F. and M. Riesz theorem
items.statement: Let $\mu$ be a finite complex Borel measure on $\mathbb T$ whose Fourier coefficients $\widehat\mu(n)=\int_{\mathbb T}\zeta^{-n}d\mu(\zeta)$ vanish for every $n<0$. Then $\mu$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $m$. More precisely, $f:=P[\mu]$ is holomorphic on $\mathbb D$ and lies in $H^1(\mathbb D)$, and if $f^*$ is the boundary function of the Fatou theorem for analytic $H^1$ then $\mu=f^*m$; consequently $|\mu|(\mathbb T)=\|f^*\|_1=\|f\|_{H^1}$.
items.strategy:
By the analyticity lemma, $f=P[\mu]$ is holomorphic and $f\in H^1$ with $\|f\|_{H^1}\le|\mu|(\mathbb T)$; also $f\in h^1$ with the same norm. The published $h^1$ representation theorem gives a unique finite measure $
u$ with $f=P[
u]$, and $(P[
u])_rm$ converges weak-star to $
u$ against continuous functions. The Fatou theorem for analytic $H^1$ gives $\|f_r-f^*\|_1	o0$, so for every continuous $g$ one has $\int g\,d
u=\lim_r\int g f_r\,dm=\int g f^*dm$. Since continuous functions separate finite measures (published uniqueness in the Riesz representation theorem), $
u=f^*m$, and then $\mu=
u$ by uniqueness of the representing measure; hence $\mu=f^*m$ is absolutely continuous. The norm identity follows from the published $h^1$ isometry and the Fatou theorem.

items.title: The H1 boundary measure is an L1 density, and the Cauchy representation
items.statement: Let $f\in H^1(\mathbb D)$ and let $\mu$ be the unique finite complex Borel measure on $\mathbb T$ with $f=P[\mu]$ (the published $h^1$ representation). Then $\mu\ll m$ and $\mu=f^*m$ for the boundary function $f^*$ of the Fatou theorem, and for every $z\in\mathbb D$ $$f(z)=P[f^*](z)=\int_{\mathbb T}P(z,\zeta)f^*(\zeta)\,dm(\zeta)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{\mathbb T}\frac{f^*(\zeta)}{\zeta-z}\,d\zeta .$$ Moreover $\|f\|_{H^1}=\|f^*\|_1=|\mu|(\mathbb T)$ and $\|f_r-f^*\|_1\to0$ as $r\uparrow1$.
items.strategy: The representing measure of an analytic $H^1$ function has vanishing negative Fourier coefficients because $f=P[\mu]$ is holomorphic; the F. and M. Riesz theorem gives $\mu=f^*m$. Then $f=P[\mu]=P[f^*]$; the norm identity is the published $h^1$ isometry combined with $|\mu|(\mathbb T)=\|f^*\|_1$, and the L1 convergence is the published Poisson-extension theorem. For the Cauchy formula, on each circle $|\zeta|=r<1$ the published Cauchy integral formula for the holomorphic $f$ gives $f(z)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{|\zeta|=r}\frac{f(\zeta)}{\zeta-z}d\zeta$ for $|z|<r$; let $r\uparrow1$ and use $\|f_r-f^*\|_1\to0$ together with the uniform boundedness of $\zeta\mapsto(\zeta-z)^{-1}$ on $\mathbb T$.

title: Analytic Hardy Spaces and Canonical Factorisation: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: Finite Blaschke products
items.statement: For $a_1,\dots,a_N\in\mathbb D$ let $B(z)=\prod_{j=1}^N b_{a_j}(z)$ be the finite Blaschke product of the normalized factors $b_a$. Then $B$ is a rational function holomorphic on an open neighbourhood of $\overline{\mathbb D}$, $|B(\zeta)|=1$ for every $\zeta\in\mathbb T$, $B(0)=\prod_{j=1}^N|a_j|$, and the zeros of $B$ in $\mathbb D$ are exactly $a_1,\dots,a_N$ with multiplicity; in particular $|B(z)|<1$ for every $z\in\mathbb D$ (a nonconstant finite Blaschke product has no interior point of modulus one). For $a_1=1/2$, $a_2=-1/2$ one computes $b_{1/2}(z)=\frac{1/2-z}{1-z/2}$ and $b_{-1/2}(z)=\frac{1/2+z}{1+z/2}$ (the normalization $\overline a/|a|$ of the second factor is $-1$), so $B(z)=b_{1/2}(z)b_{-1/2}(z)=\frac{1/4-z^2}{1-z^2/4}$, with $B(0)=1/4$ and $B(1)=B(-1)=-1$ (the latter values illustrate $|B|=1$ on the boundary).
items.strategy: Because each $b_a$ is a product of the automorphism $\varphi_a$ with the unimodular constant $\overline a/|a|$, the finite product is rational with poles outside the closed disc; the boundary identity is the modulus identity of the definition, the value at $0$ is $b_a(0)=|a|$, and the zero statement is the multiplicity clause specialized to finitely many factors. The explicit computation for $a=\pm1/2$ is direct algebra.

items.title: An infinite Blaschke product whose zeros accumulate at the boundary
items.statement: Let $a_n:=1-\frac{1}{n^2}$ for $n\ge2$. Then $\sum_{n\ge2}(1-|a_n|)=\sum_{n\ge2}\frac1{n^2}<\infty$, so $(a_n)$ is a Blaschke sequence and the Blaschke product $B=\prod_{n\ge2}b_{a_n}$ converges normally on $\mathbb D$ to a holomorphic function with $|B|\le1$, whose zeros are exactly the points $1-1/n^2$, each simple, and whose boundary function is unimodular a.e. The value at the origin is $B(0)=\prod_{n\ge2}(1-\frac1{n^2})=\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{N+1}{2N}=\frac12$. The zeros accumulate at $1\in\mathbb T$, so $B$ has no continuous extension to $\overline{\mathbb D}$ and is not a finite product. The associated $H^2$ norm is $\|B\|_{H^2}=1$, while the boundary function has modulus $1$ a.e.
items.strategy: Sum the Blaschke condition, apply the normal-convergence theorem for products with the estimate of the definition, and evaluate the telescoping product $\prod_{n=2}^N(1-\frac1{n^2})=\frac{N+1}{2N}$; the a.e. unimodularity and the zeros are clauses of the boundary-values theorem for Blaschke products.

items.title: A singular inner function generated by a point mass
items.statement: Let $\mu=\delta_1$ be the Dirac mass at the point $1\in\mathbb T$. Then $\mu$ is a finite positive measure singular with respect to $m$ and the associated function is the singular inner function $$S(z)=\exp\Bigl(-\frac{1+z}{1-z}\Bigr)\qquad(z\in\mathbb D),$$ because $K(z,1)=\frac{1+z}{1-z}$. One has $|S(z)|=e^{-P(z,1)}=e^{-(1-|z|^2)/|1-z|^2}\le1$, $S(0)=e^{-1}>0$, $S$ has no zeros in $\mathbb D$, and $|S^*(\zeta)|=1$ for every $\zeta\ne1$; in particular $|S^*|=1$ a.e. The nontangential limit of $S$ at $\zeta=1$ is $0$, because $P(z,1)\to+\infty$ along every cone at $1$. Thus $S$ is inner, nonconstant, and its boundary modulus fails to be $1$ only on the null set $\{1\}$.
items.strategy: Compute the kernel $K(z,1)$, its real part $P(z,1)$, and apply the general properties of singular inner functions; on a cone $\Gamma_A(1)$ one has $|1-z|\le(1+A)(1-|z|)$, hence $P(z,1)=\frac{1-|z|^2}{|1-z|^2}\ge\frac{1}{(1+A)^2}\cdot\frac{1-|z|^2}{(1-|z|)^2}\to+\infty$, so $S(z)\to0$ along every cone at $1$.

items.title: An outer function with a prescribed power of a vanishing modulus
items.statement:
Let $0<\alpha<\infty$ and let $h(\zeta):=|1-\zeta|^{\alpha}$ for $\zeta\in\mathbb T$ (identified with the unit circle). Then $\log h\in L^1(\mathbb T,m)$ and $h\in L^\infty(\mathbb T,m)\subseteq L^p$ for every $p$, and the associated outer function is $[h](z)=(1-z)^{\alpha}$, the principal branch normalized by $[h](0)=1$. Hence $|[h]^*(\zeta)|=|1-\zeta|^{\alpha}=h(\zeta)$ for every $\zeta
e1$, $[h]\in H^\infty(\mathbb D)$ with $\|[h]\|_\infty=2^{\alpha}$, and $[h]$ is outer; for $\alpha
otin\mathbb N$ the function $[h]$ is not rational. The identity $\int_{\mathbb T}K(z,\zeta)\log|1-\zeta|\,dm(\zeta)=\log(1-z)$ (principal branch) is the computation that produces the outer function: its real part is $\log|1-z|=P[\log|1-\zeta|](z)$ because the power series $\log(1-z)=-\sum_{n\ge1}z^n/n$ has boundary real part $\log|1-\zeta|$ with Fourier coefficients $-1/(2|n|)$, $n
e0$.
items.strategy: Compute $\int_{\mathbb T}\log|1-\zeta|dm=0$ and, more generally, the Fourier coefficients of $\log|1-\zeta|$ from $\log(1-z)=-\sum z^n/n$ by taking real parts on $|z|<1$; this identifies the Herglotz integral with $\log(1-z)$, so the outer function is $(1-z)^{\alpha}$, and the outer-function lemma supplies the modulus identity and the $H^p$ membership.

items.title: A divergent Blaschke sum: no Hardy function has these zeros
items.statement: Let $a_n:=1-\frac1n$ for $n\ge2$. Then $\sum_{n\ge2}(1-|a_n|)=\sum_{n\ge2}\frac1n=+\infty$, so $(a_n)$ is not a Blaschke sequence. Consequently: (i) there is no $f\in H^p(\mathbb D)$, $0<p\le\infty$, with $f\not\equiv0$ whose zero sequence is $(a_n)$ with the assigned multiplicities, because every such zero sequence of a nonzero $H^p$ function satisfies the Blaschke condition; (ii) the formal Blaschke product $\prod_{n\ge2}b_{a_n}$ does not converge normally on $\mathbb D$; in fact its partial products $B_N$ converge locally uniformly to the zero function, because for every fixed $z\in\mathbb D$ one has $\sum_n(1-|b_{a_n}(z)|)=+\infty$ (as $1-|b_{a_n}(z)|\ge\frac{(1-|a_n|^2)(1-|z|^2)}{2|1-\overline{a_n}z|^2}\ge\frac{c(z)}{n}$ with $c(z)>0$), so $B_N(z)\to0$, and the sequence $|B_N|$ is decreasing, so Dini's theorem upgrades pointwise convergence to local uniform convergence; (iii) by the Weierstrass product theorem on plane domains there nevertheless exists a holomorphic $f$ on $\mathbb D$, with exactly these zeros (all simple), and by (i) this $f$ lies in no $H^p$; it exhibits the failure of the boundary-uniqueness and Blaschke-factorization results outside the Hardy classes.
items.strategy: (i) contraposes the Blaschke-condition theorem. (ii) uses the identity $1-|b_a(z)|^2=\frac{(1-|a|^2)(1-|z|^2)}{|1-\overline az|^2}$ and $|1-\overline{a_n}z|\to|1-z|>0$ for fixed $z$, giving divergence of $\sum(1-|b_{a_n}(z)|)$; the partial products are decreasing in modulus, and pointwise convergence of a decreasing sequence of continuous functions to the continuous limit $0$ on a compact set is uniform (Dini). (iii) is the published zero-divisor theorem on plane domains applied to the discrete set $\{1-1/n\}\subset\mathbb D$.

items.title: Inner-outer factorization of a rational function with one interior zero
items.statement: Fix $a\in\mathbb D$, $a\ne0$, and put $$f(z):=\frac{z-a}{1-\overline a z}\cdot\frac{1+z}{2}.$$ Then $f$ is a rational function holomorphic on a neighbourhood of $\overline{\mathbb D}$; its only zero in $\mathbb D$ is $a$ (simple), its only pole is $1/\overline a$ outside the closed disc, and $|f^*|=\frac{|1+\zeta|}{2}$ on $\mathbb T$. In the normalized inner-outer factorization of [[thm-inner-outer-factorisation-hardy-space]] one has $$B=b_a,\qquad \mu=0\ \ (S_\mu=1),\qquad F(z)=\frac{1+z}{2},\qquad \lambda=-\frac{a}{|a|},$$ because $\frac{z-a}{1-\overline az}=-\frac{a}{|a|}\,b_a(z)$ and $F$ is outer with $F(0)=\frac12>0$ and $|F^*|=\frac{|1+\zeta|}{2}$. Thus $f=\lambda\,B\,F$, a pure Blaschke-times-outer factorization with trivial singular factor, and $\|f\|_{H^\infty}=\frac{3}{2}$ while $\|B\|_{H^\infty}=1$ and $\|F\|_{H^\infty}=1$.
items.strategy: Identify the zero factor with a normalized Blaschke factor up to the unimodular constant $-a/|a|$; check that $(1+z)/2$ is outer by computing $\log|(1+z)/2|=-\log2+\log|1+z|=P[\log|1+\zeta|]-\log2$ (the computation of the previous example), so the normalized outer function with modulus $|1+\zeta|/2$ is $(1+z)/2$; conclude by the uniqueness clause of the factorization theorem.

items.title: Boundary vanishing of a Hardy function is confined to a null set
items.statement: (a) The function $f(z)=1-z$ lies in $H^\infty(\mathbb D)$; its boundary function $f^*(\zeta)=1-\zeta$ vanishes exactly at $\zeta=1$, a set of $m$-measure zero, and $f\not\equiv0$. Thus a nonzero Hardy function may vanish at boundary points, although by (b) its boundary vanishing set must be null. (b) If $f\in H^p(\mathbb D)$ for some $0<p\le\infty$ and the zero set $\{f^*=0\}$ has positive $m$-measure, then $f\equiv0$. (c) (Uniqueness) If $f,g\in H^p(\mathbb D)$ have $f^*=g^*$ a.e., then $f=g$. (d) The function $f(z)=1-z$ is itself outer: it has no zeros in $\mathbb D$, its canonical factorization is $1-z=B S F$ with $B=1$, $S_\mu=1$ and $F=1-z$, and indeed $1-z=[\,|1-\zeta|\,]$ because $\log|1-z|=P[\log|1-\zeta|]$ (computed in the preceding example).
items.strategy: (a) Direct computation. (b) is the contrapositive of $\log|f^*|\in L^1$ (Riesz brothers). (c) Apply (b) to $f-g$, which lies in $H^p$ and has zero boundary function a.e. (d) $1-z$ has no zeros in $\mathbb D$ and equals $[|1-\zeta|]$-up to a unimodular factor, because its boundary modulus is $|1-\zeta|$ and it maps the disc into the half-plane $\operatorname{Re}w<1$, which is contained in a half-plane; alternatively, $\log|1-z|=P[\log|1-\zeta|]$ as computed in the outer-modulus example.
